title: Le Divorce
full_review:
Moviegoers anticipating a transporting experience from the talented directing/producing team of James Ivory and Ismail Merchant are likely to be disappointed with their latest offering, the superficial drama "Le Divorce" (Fox Searchlight).

The duo is most known for their period dramas such as "The Remains of the Day" and "Howards End," although director Ivory has ventured into the modern setting a few times with mixed success. Billed as a comedy of manners, "Le Divorce" is set in present-day Paris where young California gal Isabel (Kate Hudson) arrives to visit her pregnant sister Roxeanne (Naomi Watts). Roxeanne has just been jilted by her philandering French husband Charles-Henri (Melvil Poupaud), hence the movie's title.

Based on the novel by Diane Johnson, the film endeavors to highlight the differences between Americans and the French, especially when it comes to manners, morals, affairs of the heart, money and even food. But the story is disappointingly shallow and surprisingly dark at turns, with underdeveloped characters that fail to involve the audience. As the clunky film laboriously chugs along, the viewer cares less and less about the characters.

The story's main thread is Isabel and her transformation from valley girl to sophisticate. But Hudson does not have the acting chops to convey Isabel's interior metamorphosis. The change is solely exterior: from gauzy, bohemian shirts to stylish suits and smartly tied scarves, from long flowing curls to a chic bob. She begins an affair with her brother-in-law's older uncle Edgar (Thierry Lhermitte). But their interactions
(older-man-teaching-younger-woman-the-ways-of-the-world) feel forced and artificial.

Ivory and writing partner Ruth Prawer Jhabvala adapted the novel for the screen, but did not capture the essence of the characters or the story. They could not bring together in a convincing or involving manner the plot's many strands that range from a family squabble over a famous painting of St. Ursula by Georges de La Tour to Charles-Henri's affair with a Russian woman. One gets the sense that there is so much more to each of these characters that has been simplified (and therefore made much less interesting) for the screen.

Merchant and Ivory have assembled a talented group of actors for their ensemble cast, but the material is deficient, so none of them offer more than a standard performance. Leslie Caron stars as a stereotypical French matriarch, protecting the honor of her family through guile and manipulation. Sam Waterston and Stockard Channing are Isabel and Roxeanne's more straightforward parents who fly in from Santa Barbara to be with their daughters. Bebe Neuwirth plays an American museum expert and Glenn Close is a writer who secretly had an affair with Edgar years ago. Matthew Modine, whose performance is just a couple of frames past a cameo appearance, plays an erratic jealous American husband.

Although meant as yet another way in which the French and Americans differ, viewers may be dismayed by the casual attitude the characters take toward marital commitment. The foil to this is Roxeanne, who, faced with a divorce, has seemingly undergone a change of heart when it comes to morals. She is sickened by the casualness with which her in-laws discuss "adultery and fornication" and as a result becomes the movie's moral compass.

The settings are intimate and beautiful, but, without an absorbing story, they are little more than the pretty packaging of an empty box.

Some subtitles.

Because of extramarital affairs, a few implied sexual encounters, brief violence and fleeting profanity and crass language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
